power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: The rapid, unregulated expansion of the call center industry in developing countries has increased occupational health risks for young adults, particularly with regard to auditory health.

Prolonged exposure to acoustic trauma, long working hours, and the high intensity nature of call center work can negatively affect young adults at the start of their working lives and may contribute to permanent noise induced hearing loss (NIHL).
This damage is often irreversible but preventable if identified at an early stage.
This study aims to evaluate the burden of auditory impairment among call center employees in Egypt and to propose evidence based mitigation strategies.
Methods A pilot cross sectional study was conducted among employees of various medical call centers over approximately three months (January to March 2026).
Participants were recruited through voluntary (self selected) sampling.
Data were collected using a structured questionnaire on work history, and statistical analysis was performed to examine associations with work duration and intensity.
Three semi structured, open ended interviews were conducted in March 2026 to explore the symptoms in greater depth.
Forty six call center employees completed the questionnaire.

The most frequently reported symptoms were mishearing words (82.6%), difficulty understanding speech in background noise (80.4%), needing others to repeat themselves (78.3%), and sensitivity to loud sounds (78.3%); 60.9% reported tinnitus.

Higher auditory symptom severity was associated with a history of acoustic shock (Mann Whitney U = 344.0, p = .004) and with greater cognitive symptom burden (Spearman's ρ = .416, p = .004), but not significantly with shift type (p = .177), years of work (p = .885), or daily and weekly working hours.
Qualitative interviews described auditory strain that builds through the shift, disrupted sleep, informal coping, and the absence of employer guidance or symptom reporting pathways.

Self reported auditory symptoms were common in this preliminary sample of call center employees and were associated with acoustic shock exposure and cognitive symptom burden, but not significantly with shift pattern or length of service.
Because the study was cross sectional, relied on self reports, and used a small volunteer sample (pilot study), the findings cannot establish causation or true prevalence.

Recommended measures include acoustic shock limiters with incident reporting, audiometric screening that prioritizes at risk employees, safe volume education with regular breaks, and educational programs on auditory hazards and early warning signs to prevent actual auditory damage.
Larger multi site studies with audiometric confirmation are also needed.
Noise is defined as unwanted and disturbing sound (Occupational Safety and Health Administration, 2002).

text.text: Although occupational hearing loss is traditionally associated with the mining and manufacturing industries, the digital transformation of the global economy has created new high risk groups, most notably call center operators handling various accounts.
Regardless of the industry, the resulting damage is the same: progressive hearing loss.

In developing countries, economic instability and limited employment opportunities push young adults and recent graduates toward careers in the telecommunications sector, particularly call center services.
These roles are accessible because of minimal entry requirements and competitive wages compared with other service sectors, which makes them attractive short term employment options for young people.

Call center employees frequently work long shifts with rotating schedules, which may disrupt circadian rhythm and impair melatonin secretion, causing chronic fatigue and elevated blood pressure (James et al., 2017), along with a high incidence of psychological distress, anxiety, and burnout.

text.text: From an auditory perspective, continuous exposure to unregulated noise from calls, call disconnections, and unexpected high intensity acoustic signals are stressors that may increase the risk of noise induced hearing loss (NIHL), tinnitus, and central auditory processing dysfunction.

Despite the rapid expansion of the call center industry, particularly with Egypt emerging as a regional hub for business process outsourcing and customer service operations, research on noise induced hearing loss among call center operators remains limited, particularly in the Middle East and Egypt.
Previous studies have addressed related concerns in different populations (Pawlaczyk Luszczynska et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Previous studies have addressed related concerns in different populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Pawlaczyk Luszczynska et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: For example, a study of call center operators in a European setting found that most operators had normal hearing, although a meaningful minority showed early high frequency notching despite reporting auditory and visual symptoms.
This highlights the importance of subjective symptom reporting, since symptoms may occur before measurable hearing loss is detected, and the need for further studies.
However, that study was conducted in a European context and did not specifically examine occupational hearing among call center workers in Egypt.

Similarly, a recent review (Chen & Su, 2025) focused primarily on the mechanisms of auditory damage and noise induced hearing loss in broader workplace populations rather than specifically examining call center employees.

text.text: Furthermore, limited attention has been given to the psychological and cognitive strain that may accompany auditory symptoms, and to early subjective indicators that may precede clinically detectable hearing impairment.

This gap directly shaped the objectives of the present study, which aimed to determine the prevalence and severity of self reported auditory symptoms among call center employees in Egypt and to identify the occupational and lifestyle factors that may be strongly associated with symptom severity.

Rather than relying solely on audiometric assessment, the study adopted a symptom based approach to capture early auditory complaints and their relationship with cognitive and psychological symptom burden.
The findings provide additional evidence from an understudied occupational population and suggest that auditory symptoms may be highly prevalent among call center employees.

In the present sample, approximately 80% of participants reported mishearing and difficulty understanding speech in background noise, while a history of acoustic shock emerged as one of the strongest correlates of symptom severity.

A significant association was also observed between auditory and cognitive symptom burden, suggesting that auditory difficulties among call center employees may extend beyond hearing related complaints alone.
The main objective of the study was to evaluate the extent of auditory dysfunction among call center operators in Egypt and to investigate the factors that may influence its prevalence and severity.
The specific objectives were: 1.
To identify the prevalence of self reported auditory dysfunction among call center employees, including tinnitus, difficulty hearing in background noise, and other early symptoms of hearing loss.
To assess the severity and pattern of hearing impairment, including which ear is more affected.
To examine the association between shift work and auditory dysfunction, focusing on whether night or rotating shifts increase the risk or severity.
To detect early warning signs and patterns of auditory and cognitive impairment, enabling early intervention and prevention strategies.
To explore lifestyle and occupational factors that contribute to auditory risk, including duration of headset use, personal audio device use, smoking, and past medical history.
To provide evidence based recommendations for mitigating noise related hearing damage in call center environments, including occupational health guidelines and employee awareness strategies.
This is a pilot cross sectional study with a mixed methods component (a questionnaire survey and open ended interviews).

 Descriptive statistics were calculated to summarize the demographic characteristics, occupational exposure (e.g., work hours, shift type, headset use), and auditory symptoms.
Measures included range, mean, standard deviation, frequencies, and percentages.
Ninety five percent confidence intervals for proportions were calculated using the Wilson score method.
 Individual symptom items were dichotomized into present/absent for prevalence estimates.

Composite auditory (seven items) and cognitive (four items) symptom severity scores were calculated as the sum of the item scores, and their distributions were assessed with the Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Shapiro-Wilk tests.
Analyses used available cases (one participant had missing cognitive data).

 Because symptom items are ordinal and several subgroups were small and unbalanced (e.g., five day shift employees), nonparametric tests were used: Spearman's rank correlation for associations between symptom severity and continuous or ordinal exposures, the Mann-Whitney U test for two group comparisons (e.g., acoustic shock yes/no), and the Kruskal-Wallis H test for comparisons across three or more groups (e.g., day, night, and rotating shift).

The test showed no significant difference in cognitive symptom severity across shift categories (H(2) = 0.851, p = .653, n = 45), and the null hypothesis was retained.
This mirrors the finding for auditory symptom severity by shift (Section 1.5, p = .177): neither auditory nor cognitive symptom burden differed meaningfully by shift schedule in this sample.

Taken together, shift timing does not appear to be a driving factor behind either symptom domain, reinforcing that acoustic shock exposure and the auditory-cognitive symptom link (Sections 1.4 and 1.6) are more informative targets for prevention than shift pattern.

As with the auditory comparison, the small and unbalanced subgroup sizes (day shift, n = 5) limit the power of this test to detect a true difference, so this should be interpreted as an absence of evidence for a shift effect rather than confirmed evidence of no effect.

Three semi structured, open ended interviews (Participants 1, 2, and 3) were conducted in March 2026 using an interview guide adapted from questions used in the published literature (Appendix 2).

The guide covered four a priori topic areas: (1) perceived auditory strain and fatigue, (2) sleep disturbance due to night shifts, (3) anxiety, mental fatigue, coping strategies, and headset use habits, and (4) unreported or subtle symptoms.
Transcripts were bilingual (Arabic-English) and machine transcribed.

Two of the three transcripts (those of Participants 2 and 3) contained substantial automatic speech recognition (ASR) errors and unsegmented speech, so close paraphrase was used instead of direct quotation for those sections, consistent with standard practice for degraded qualitative data.
Analysis followed Braun and Clarke's (2006) six phase approach to thematic analysis: familiarization, initial coding, theme searching, theme review, theme definition and naming, and write up.
Participants: P1customer service/back office agent (fixed day shift, later flexible hours); P2call center agent (rotating shifts); P3sales agent (rotating/night shifts, high pressure targets).
All three participants described a clear within shift trajectory rather than a static level of discomfortsymptoms were mild or absent at shift start and intensified toward the end.

P1 distinguished a high volume "frontline" role (constant, back to back calls) from a self paced back office role and reported that auditory and physical fatigue ("awful headaches," needing painkillers) were markedly worse during the frontline period.

P3 similarly linked ear pain directly to shift progression, describing mild discomfort early on that became a "slight pain" by the end of the shift, and explicitly confirmed that this was shift related rather than incidental.
Both P2 and P3 reported raising the headset volume as the shift progressed in order to keep understanding callers.
P3 described pushing the volume to very high levels through a browser extension in the later hours of the shift, framing it as a direct response to reduced clarity rather than a stable preference.
Sub theme 1.3 -Tinnitus, pressure, and ear clogging sensations.

P1 reported a progression from occasional muffled hearing to persistent ringing (tinnitus) that continued even after leaving the job, alongside a sensation of pressure or clogging localized to the ear kept under the headset.
This was severe enough to prompt a medical visit, but the examination performed (visual otoscopy) did not include audiometric or frequency testing.
This is a methodological gap, since no objective threshold data exist to corroborate the self report.
P2 and P3 reported pressure sensations during or after calls but were less certain about buzzing specifically; they noted that symptoms correlated with, and increased with, shift intensity.

Theme 2: Sleep Is Structurally Disrupted by Shift Demands, Independent of "Night Shift" Framing Sleep disruption was reported across all three participants, but the mechanism differed by role rather than by a simple day/night distinction.

P1 reported that sleep was largely stable during a hybrid schedule but deteriorated once physical, symptom related discomfort (ear pressure) began to interfere, more than because of the shift timing itself.

P3 reported a much sharper effect: sleep dropped from a baseline of about 9 hours to 5-6 hours of poor quality sleep under a full overnight schedule, and P3 described daytime recovery sleep as never equivalent to true rest.
P2 described the lack of a clear sleep schedule, difficulty coping with shift work, and progressively decreasing sleep hours.

P3 linked poor sleep directly to reduced work performance in a role that "needs you to be...full of energy," and to broader emotional overload and a reduced capacity to manage daily life outside work.
P1 did not report the same degree of cognitive or mood impact from sleep specifically, attributing daytime tiredness more to cumulative workload than to sleep loss per se.
Sub theme 3.1 -Anxiety tied to income and performance stability.

P3, who works in a target driven sales role, reported that anxiety was conditional on performance ("when I'm doing well at work I don't feel that anxious") and directly linked poor sleep and fatigue to fear over job and income stability.
On the structured symptom checklist, P3 confirmed difficulty concentrating and trouble sleeping but denied most somatic anxiety symptoms (sweating, trembling, palpitations).

P3 described concrete downstream effects, including missed social plans and difficulty attending personal obligations, and attributed these explicitly to rotating and overnight shift patterns rather than to the sales role alone.

P1's account (customer service, not commission or target based) framed the stress as diffuse and comparative ("stressful from all sides": study, work, and life stage) rather than attributing it to a single dominant cause.
P1 also noted that colleagues who treated the job as a primary income source seemed comparatively more at ease with the workload.
Sub theme 4.1 -Self directed micro breaks.
P1 described discretionary strategies, such as stepping away from the desk, eating, and taking short naps, used opportunistically rather than as part of any structured break policy.

P3 reported becoming a heavy smoker and relying on caffeine (espresso shots) specifically to manage shift induced exhaustion, framing this as a direct coping response to the energy demands of the sales role.
Sub theme 4.3 -Unilateral headset use as informal ear "resting."

Both P1 and P2 reported habitually keeping one ear free of the headset (typically the non dominant or left ear) to preserve situational awareness, switching sides when the free ear became uncomfortable.
This suggests an unprompted, self taught compensatory behavior rather than anything trained or company issued.
All participants independently confirmed that no formal guidance existed on headset volume limits or break frequency.
P1 noted that the headset hardware had a built in, color coded loudness indicator, but no policy enforced attention to it.
P3 confirmed this and added that management actively discouraged removing headsets rather than encouraging rest breaks.
Theme 5: Symptoms Are Underreported and Normalized as "Part of the Job" Sub theme 5.1 -No formal reporting pathway used.
None of the participants had proactively reported hearing related symptoms through any formal channel (occupational health, HR, or a doctor specifically citing work) before this study.
P1's medical visit was self initiated outside any workplace process, and P3 explicitly confirmed that hearing or ear problems had "never" been raised with anyone before this discussion.
Sub theme 5.2 -Peer level awareness without escalation.

P3 confirmed noticing similar struggles among coworkers, describing colleagues as "struggling" and "tired," but reported that this was discussed informally among peers ("that's how I go") rather than escalated.
This is consistent with a workplace culture that treats these symptoms as an expected cost of the job rather than as an occupational health signal.

Across all three accounts, auditory strain presents as a cumulative, within shift phenomenon compounded by unmanaged compensatory volume increases and occurring in a policy vacuum in which no employer guidance on safe headset use exists.
Sleep disruption and psychological load appear to interact with auditory symptoms, rather than operating independently of them, particularly in high pressure, target driven roles.

Critically, symptom reporting is almost entirely absent from formal channels, which suggests that surveys and self report instruments that rely on participants having already raised concerns with a doctor or employer will substantially undercount prevalence.

This supports the study's premise that a psychological and behavioral early symptom pathway (tinnitus, subjective muffling, perceived ear pressure) may be more sensitive than threshold based audiometry in this population, and it reinforces the case for pairing self report data with objective audiometric testing rather than relying on either alone.

text.text: This study examined self reported auditory dysfunction and its correlates among 46 call center employees in Egypt.

Consistent with the study's first objective, auditory symptoms were highly prevalent: more than three quarters of employees reported mishearing words, difficulty following speech in noise, needing conversations repeated, and heightened sensitivity to loud sounds, and roughly six in ten reported tinnitus.

This symptom profile is consistent with early, subclinical auditory strain rather than frank hearing loss, and is broadly in line with what would be expected in an occupational group with prolonged daily headset use and continuous exposure to call related acoustic stimuli.

The composite auditory severity score was approximately normally distributed around a moderate level of symptom burden, with a smaller subset of employees reporting markedly elevated scores (up to 33 out of the composite maximum).

This right leaning spread suggests that while most employees experience a low to moderate symptom load, a minority may be experiencing a more concentrated pattern of auditory strain -a group that would benefit most from targeted screening.

Of all the occupational and medical variables tested, a self reported history of acoustic shocka sudden, unexpectedly loud sound transmitted through the headset -showed by far the strongest and most consistent association with auditory symptom severity, both as a correlate (ρ = .414, p = .004) and as a group comparison (p = .004).

This aligns with the broader occupational health literature on call center and telecommunications workers, where acoustic shock incidents (e.g., feedback squeals, line faults, or malicious loud noises from callers) have been identified as a distinct hazard separate from routine background noise exposure (McFerran & Baguley, 2007; Westcott, 2006).

text.text: The magnitude of this association, in a modest sample, suggests acoustic shock history may be a more sensitive marker of at risk employees than conventional exposure metrics such as years of service or shift pattern -both of which showed negligible correlations with symptom severity in this dataset (ρ = .022 and non significant shift comparison, respectively).

The significant correlation between auditory and cognitive symptom severity (ρ = .416, p = .004), driven most strongly by slowed information processing (ρ = .500, p < .001), is consistent with the concept of listening effort: when auditory processing is compromised, cognitive resources are redirected toward decoding speech and monitoring sound, leaving less capacity for other cognitive tasks and manifesting as fatigue, slowed processing, and difficulty concentrating.

text.text: In a call center setting, where accurate real time listening under noisy conditions is central to job performance, this auditory-cognitive coupling has direct implications for both employee wellbeing and operational performance (e.g., error rates, handle time).
The borderline associations for headache and concentration difficulty (p = .053-.061) likely reflect the same underlying mechanism and may reach significance in a larger sample.

Contrary to some prior assumptions, shift type was not significantly associated with auditory symptom severity (p = .177), suggesting that when shift is treated as a simple three category variable, it does not capture meaningful variation in auditory risk in this cohort.

This may indicate that cumulative or event based exposures (such as acoustic shock or headset volume habits) are more proximally related to symptom severity than the time of day pattern of work itself, or it may reflect limited statistical power to detect a true shift effect.

Similarly, years of work and daily/weekly work hour categories showed negligible correlations with severity, which may reflect adaptation over time, survivorship (more severely affected employees may have already left the role), or simply that these coarse categorical exposure measures do not capture cumulative noise dose with sufficient precision.
Headphone/device volume (p = .065) and middle ear disease history (p = .072) both showed trends toward higher severity that did not reach the conventional significance threshold.

Given the small size of some subgroups (e.g., only 10 employees reported ear disease), these should be interpreted as hypothesis generating rather than null findings, and would benefit from confirmation in a larger sample.

Likewise, the medical history variables that showed no association (cholesterol, hypertension, head trauma) had very small affected subgroups (n = 2-5), so the absence of a significant result more likely reflects insufficient power than a true absence of effect and should not be over interpreted as reassuring.
• Cross sectional design: causal or temporal relationships (e.g., whether acoustic shock precedes or follows symptom onset) cannot be established.

• All outcome and exposure measures were self reported; no audiometric testing (pure tone audiometry) was performed to objectively confirm hearing status, so findings reflect perceived rather than measured auditory function.
• Modest overall sample size (N = 46), and several subgroup comparisons involved very small cell sizes (n = 2-10), limiting statistical power to detect true associations for several variables.
• Single center/single country sample, which may limit generalizability to call center workforces with different equipment, noise control policies, or work cultures.
• Recall bias is possible for retrospective exposure items such as acoustic shock history and years of work.

• Composite severity scores, while normally distributed, combine heterogeneous symptoms into a single score, which may obscure symptom specific patterns; nonparametric tests were used throughout for consistency, which is a conservative but not the only defensible analytic choice given the approximately normal distribution of the composite scores.
• Objective audiometric testing was not performed.

This decision was informed by prior literature indicating that hearing loss in this occupational population typically does not reach diagnostic clinical thresholds (Pawlaczyk Luszczynska et al., 2018); the study therefore prioritized capturing patient reported auditory and stress symptoms, which may be more sensitive to early or subclinical occupational effects than audiometry alone.
However, this means the study cannot confirm or rule out measurable hearing loss in participants, and self reported symptoms are subject to recall and reporting bias.

The achieved sample size (n=46) was below the a priori target of 100-120 because reaching the target was not logistically feasible within the data collection period of almost three months; the study is therefore a pilot study, and the small sample limits statistical power and the precision of subgroup comparisons; findings should be interpreted as preliminary.

Voluntary (self selected) sampling restricted to three companies via WhatsApp introduces potential selection and non response bias, and many of those reached did not complete the questionnaire, limiting generalizability to the broader call center workforce in Egypt • Multiple group comparisons were performed at α = .05 without correction for multiplicity, and the sample size did not allow multivariable adjustment for potential confounders (e.g., age, sleep duration, headphone use outside work); the acoustic shock association is therefore best regarded as exploratory.
• There was no comparison group of non call center workers, so the observed symptom frequencies cannot be attributed to call center work alone.
The qualitative component comprised only three discussions, and the machine transcribed Arabic-English recordings contained transcription errors, limiting the depth and transferability of the themes

In line with the study's sixth objective, these findings support several practical, evidence based recommendations for hearing conservation in call center environments: • Implement or verify acoustic shock (loud noise burst) limiters on all headsets, and establish a formal incident reporting pathway so acoustic shock events are logged and followed up with hearing checks.
• Introduce periodic audiometric screening for employees, prioritizing those who report acoustic shock events or high symptom burden on routine surveys.
• Incorporate brief cognitive symptom screening (e.g., concentration, fatigue) alongside auditory symptom checks, given their observed correlation, to catch early listening effort related strain.
• Provide employee education on safe headset volume levels and encourage regular listening breaks, particularly for employees who report several hours of daily headset use.

• Given the high overall prevalence of early symptoms, consider organization wide awareness campaigns on early warning signs of noise related auditory strain, rather than targeting only high tenure or night shift employees specifically.

In this pilot cross sectional study of 46 call center employees in Greater Cairo, which relied on self reported symptoms, auditory symptoms were common: more than three quarters of participants reported mishearing words, difficulty understanding speech in background noise, needing others to repeat themselves, and sensitivity to loud sounds, and about six in ten reported tinnitus.

Symptom severity was most clearly associated with a history of acoustic shock (p = .004) and with concurrent cognitive symptom burden (ρ = .416, p = .004), whereas shift type, years of work, and working hours showed no significant association.

Because the subgroups were small and unbalanced (only five day shift employees), a shift effect cannot be excluded, and the borderline trends for headset/device volume (p = .065) and middle ear disease history (p = .072) warrant testing in larger samples.

Themes from the interviews were consistent with these findings, describing auditory strain that builds over the shift, compensatory increases in headset volume, disrupted sleep, and no employer guidance or reporting pathway for hearing related symptoms.

These findings should be read as preliminary associations rather than causal effects: the design was cross sectional, all measures were self reported without audiometry, the sample was a self selected volunteer sample smaller than planned (pilot study), and there was no comparison group, so the true prevalence of hearing loss among call center workers cannot be inferred.
Even so, they identify acute acoustic events and cumulative listening load, rather than shift schedule or tenure, as the most practical targets for prevention.

Acoustic shock limiters with incident reporting, audiometric screening that prioritizes employees with shock events or high symptom burden, safe volume education, and regular listening breaks are recommended, and larger multi site studies pairing symptom questionnaires with audiometry are needed to confirm these results.
The response patterns and effect sizes from this pilot study can inform sample size planning for that larger study.
